slides.title: Indicators of Malicious Activity
points: The exam may give you a symptom instead of an attack name. Use the indicator to infer what is happening.
Security+ Objective 2.4: given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.

slides.title: Account Lockout
slides.teach: An account becomes locked after failed authentication attempts or a security policy trigger.

course.learn: An account becomes locked after failed authentication attempts or a security policy trigger.

breakdown.explanation: Too many failed attempts cause the account to lock.

course.example: Many accounts lock after repeated failed logins.
course.check_q: Which indicator occurs after excessive failed logins?

slides.title: Concurrent Session Usage
slides.teach: The same account is active in multiple sessions or locations at the same time.

course.learn: The same account is active in multiple sessions or locations at the same time.

breakdown.explanation: One account appears to be used simultaneously.

course.why: Unexpected concurrent sessions may indicate stolen credentials.
course.example: One user has sessions from unrelated networks at the same time.
course.exam: Same account, same time → CONCURRENT SESSION.
course.check_q: Which indicator describes simultaneous use of one account?

slides.title: Blocked Content
slides.teach: Security controls prevent access to content, destinations, files, or traffic.

course.learn: Security controls prevent access to content, destinations, files, or traffic.
course.why: Blocked content can reveal attempted access to risky resources.
course.example: A web filter repeatedly blocks a malicious domain.
course.exam: Security control stopped it → BLOCKED CONTENT.
course.check_q: Which indicator describes content prevented by a security control?

slides.title: Impossible Travel
slides.teach: Authentication occurs from geographically distant locations in a time window that makes normal travel impossible.

course.learn: Authentication occurs from geographically distant locations in a time window that makes normal travel impossible.

breakdown.explanation: The account moves faster than a person could travel.

course.why: It can indicate stolen credentials or tokens.
course.example: Successful logins occur from distant countries fifteen minutes apart.
course.exam: Can't travel that fast → IMPOSSIBLE TRAVEL.
course.check_q: Which indicator involves impossible geographic login movement?

slides.title: Resource Consumption
slides.teach: Unexpectedly high CPU, memory, bandwidth, disk, or other resource usage.

course.learn: Unexpectedly high CPU, memory, bandwidth, disk, or other resource usage.
course.why: High usage may indicate malware or DoS activity.
course.example: Web-server bandwidth suddenly saturates with abnormal traffic.
course.check_q: Which indicator describes unexpectedly high resource usage?

slides.title: Resource Inaccessibility
slides.teach: A system, file, or service becomes unavailable or unreachable.

course.learn: A system, file, or service becomes unavailable or unreachable.

breakdown.explanation: Users cannot access something they normally can.

course.why: Loss of access may indicate ransomware or DoS.
course.example: Employees cannot open shared files after malware runs.
course.check_q: Which indicator is loss of access to files or services?

slides.title: Out-of-cycle Logging
slides.teach: Logs or events appear at unusual times or outside expected operational cycles.

course.learn: Logs or events appear at unusual times or outside expected operational cycles.

breakdown.explanation: Activity happens when it normally should not.
Admin login at 3 AM, Unexpected job run

course.why: Unexpected timing can indicate unauthorized activity.
course.example: Admin actions appear overnight with no scheduled maintenance.
course.check_q: Which indicator involves events outside expected times?

slides.title: Published / Documented Indicators
slides.teach: Known indicators published by vendors, ISACs, threat-intelligence sources, or security documentation.

course.learn: Known indicators published by vendors, ISACs, threat-intelligence sources, or security documentation.

breakdown.explanation: The indicator is already known and documented.
Known bad hash, Documented malicious IP

course.why: Known indicators accelerate detection and correlation.
course.example: A host contacts an IP listed in a trusted threat-intelligence feed.
course.check_q: Which indicator is matched against a known malicious hash or IP?

slides.title: Missing Logs
slides.teach: Expected logs are absent, deleted, disabled, or incomplete.

course.learn: Expected logs are absent, deleted, disabled, or incomplete.

breakdown.explanation: The records that should exist are gone.

course.why: Attackers may remove logs to hide activity.
course.example: Authentication logs are missing during the incident window.
course.exam: Where did the logs go? → MISSING LOGS.
course.check_q: Which indicator describes expected audit records being absent?

blocks.title: Read the symptom first
items: Seattle then Europe minutes later → IMPOSSIBLE TRAVEL
The account appears in locations a person could not reach in time.
Example: Successful logins occur from distant countries 15 minutes apart.
Same account active twice → CONCURRENT SESSION
Multiple simultaneous sessions may indicate stolen credentials.
Example: One account is active on unrelated networks.
Unexpected resource spikes can indicate malicious activity.
Files or service unavailable → RESOURCE INACCESSIBILITY
The observable symptom is loss of access.
Example: Employees can no longer open shared files.
Expected audit records disappear → MISSING LOGS
Attackers may delete or disable logs to hide activity.
Example: Authentication logs are missing during the incident window.
The indicator has already been documented by a trusted intelligence source.
Example: A host contacts an IP listed in threat intelligence.
blocks.example: Memory: Lockout · Concurrent · Blocked · Impossible travel · Resource spike · Inaccessible · Wrong time · Known IOC · Missing logs.

questions.q: Many accounts lock after repeated failed login attempts. Which indicator is most direct?
questions.explanation: The observed indicator is the accounts becoming locked.

questions.q: One account has active sessions from two unrelated networks at the same time. Which indicator best fits?
questions.explanation: The same account is being used simultaneously.

questions.q: A user logs in from Seattle and then London fifteen minutes later. Which indicator best fits?
questions.explanation: The geographic movement is not physically possible in that time.

questions.q: A web server suddenly consumes nearly all available bandwidth. Which indicator best fits?
questions.explanation: The key symptom is unexpectedly high resource usage.

questions.q: Employees can no longer open shared files after malware executes. Which indicator best fits?
questions.explanation: The primary symptom is loss of access.

questions.q: Administrative activity appears at 3 AM with no scheduled work. Which indicator best fits?
questions.explanation: The event occurs outside expected operational timing.

questions.q: A host connects to an IP already listed as malicious in a trusted threat-intelligence feed. Which indicator best fits?
questions.explanation: The IP is a known documented indicator.

questions.q: Authentication logs are absent during the incident window. Which indicator is most concerning?
